blocks.title: Definitions
blocks.content:
Unless otherwise specified, the terms defined here apply as used in this operational handbook. They 
may have different meanings in other contexts.
Active (tuberculosis) case-finding: Provider-initiated screening and testing in communities by 
mobile teams, often using mobile X-ray and rapid molecular tests. The term is sometimes used 
synonymously with “systematic screening”.
Adherence: Extent to which a person’s behaviour (e.g. taking medicines, following a particular diet, 
changing lifestyle) corresponds with agreed recommendations from a health care provider.
Advanced HIV disease: For ado

summary.text: Defines key terms used in the child and adolescent TB operational handbook, such as active case-finding, adherence, advanced HIV disease and adverse events. It goes on through diagnostic, treatment, disease severity and programme terms, ending with definitions of treatment outcomes, the tuberculin skin test and TB disease. Footnotes cite WHO reporting frameworks and outcome definitions.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content: 1. Introduction

summary.text: A heading for chapter 1, the introduction.

blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Tuberculosis (TB) is a preventable and curable disease, but it continues to impact the lives and 
development of millions of children and adolescents. Children and young adolescents aged under 
15 years represent about 11% of all TB cases globally. This means 1.1 million children and young 
adolescents aged under 15 years fall ill with TB every year (1).
National tuberculosis programmes (NTPs) notify less than half of these children, and there is a large 
case detection gap of children who are not diagnosed and/or not reported. The gap is largest in 
children aged under 5 years. Reasons for th

summary.text: Notes that children and young adolescents under 15 make up about 11% of TB cases, or 1.1 million a year, but fewer than half are notified, with the largest gap in children under 5 owing to diagnostic difficulties. It introduces the 2022 consolidated guidelines and defines a child as under 10 and an adolescent as 10–19 years.

blocks.title: Children and adolescents as a key vulnerable population
blocks.content:
population
Children can present with TB disease at any age, but most commonly between the ages of 1 and 
4 years in high TB burden settings. Children who develop TB disease usually do so within a year of 
TB infection. The presentation of TB in children is an indicator of recent and ongoing transmission of 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the community (4).
Infants and young children, especially those aged under 2 years, are at higher risk of developing 
disseminated disease and tuberculosis meningitis (TBM), which are associated with high morbidity and 
mortality (4). Adolescents with TB usuall

summary.text: Explains that TB in children is most common at ages 1–4, usually follows recent infection and signals ongoing community transmission, that infants face high risk of severe disease, and that adolescents often have adult-type disease and particular psychosocial needs.

blocks.title: Rationale and objectives of this operational handbook
blocks.content:
handbook
The aim of this operational handbook is to provide practical guidance on the implementation of the 
World Health Organization (WHO) policy recommendations on the prevention and management 
of TB in children and adolescents under programmatic circumstances and at different levels of the 
health system.
The practical guidance aims to inform the development or revision of national policies and related 
implementation guidance (e.g. handbooks, standard operating procedures) on the management of 
TB in children and adolescents. This handbook can also help countries adequately plan for the

summary.text: States that the handbook aims to give practical guidance on implementing WHO recommendations on child and adolescent TB and to inform national policies and capacity building. It cites the UN high-level meeting targets for treating children with TB and providing preventive treatment.

•	 inform dissemination approaches.

blocks.title: Target audience
blocks.content:
The target audience for this handbook includes NTPs and other child health programmes that provide 
care for children with or at risk of TB, including maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health 
programmes, HIV services, and PHC programmes. The handbook also targets paediatricians and 
other health care workers (HCWs) in the public and private sectors, school health services, civil society 
and community-based organizations, and health care educators.

summary.text: Identifies the handbook's audience as national TB programmes, child health, HIV and primary care programmes, paediatricians and other health workers, schools, civil society and educators.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
About a quarter of the world’s population has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The 
vast majority of these people do not have TB disease (10). It is estimated that 7.5 million children 
and young adolescents aged under 15 years are newly infected with M. tuberculosis each year (11). 
Cumulatively, about 67 million children and young adolescents aged under 15 years are infected 
with M. tuberculosis, including 2 million with MDR-TB and 100 000 with extensively drug-resistant 
tuberculosis (XDR-TB) strains, and therefore at risk of developing TB disease (12). The risk of infection

2.2.1. Prioritizing household contacts
House

summary.text: Describes contact investigation for children and adolescents, stressing that household and close contacts of people with pulmonary TB should be systematically screened and citing the high risk of disease in infected young children without preventive treatment. It covers prioritising household contacts and planning and budgeting for facility- and community-based approaches. Country examples and boxes describe implementation experiences, including challenges such as reaching remote households and stigma. It ends with prerequisites for a community-based model from the CONTACT study in Uganda and Cameroon.

blocks.title: TB screening approaches in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
adolescents
Screening serves to identify children and adolescents who may have TB disease (presumptive TB) 
and who need further evaluation to make or confirm a TB diagnosis (see Chapter 4). It also helps to 
identify children and adolescents who are eligible for and could benefit from TPT. A screening test is 
not intended to be a diagnostic tool. People with positive results on a screening test should undergo 
further diagnostic evaluation.
Children and adolescents living with HIV should be systematically screened for TB disease at each 
visit to a health facility. Child and adolescent house

summary.text: Explains the purpose of TB screening in children and adolescents and when it should be done, such as at every visit for those living with HIV and during contact investigation for household contacts. It describes screening tools, including symptom screening, chest X-ray and rapid molecular tests, and their use by age group. It covers practical considerations for screening child close contacts, including caregiver preferences. It ends by explaining when chest X-ray is needed before starting preventive treatment.

blocks.title: Screening children and adolescents living with HIV
blocks.content:
HIV
Children living with HIV have a high risk of rapid progression to severe disease and death if a diagnosis 
of TB is missed. A child living with HIV is 3.5 times more likely to progress to TB disease than a child who 
is HIV-negative (29). The risk, although greatly reduced, remains elevated in children on antiretroviral 
therapy (ART). An estimated 10% of paediatric deaths from TB are among children living with HIV, 
with 21 000 deaths annually (1). It is for this reason that WHO strongly recommends that children 
living with HIV are screened for TB.
2.4.1. Screening for symptoms and conta

summary.text: Describes TB screening of children living with HIV, who are at much higher risk of progression and death, using a symptom and contact screen at every visit with an algorithm and noted sensitivity and specificity. It covers other screening tests, implementation and screening of adolescents, and closes with key points on screening.

summary.text: Introduces chapter 3 on preventing TB in children and adolescents through BCG vaccination, preventive treatment and infection control, with a pathway figure.

blocks.title: BCG vaccination
blocks.content:
BCG is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis that was originally isolated 
in 1902 from a tuberculous cow. BCG has demonstrated significant effectiveness, but protection has 
not been consistent against all forms of TB in all age groups. BCG has also shown effectiveness in 
preventing leprosy (caused by Mycobacterium leprae) and Buruli ulcer (caused by Mycobacterium 
ulcerans) (31).
BCG provides good (up to 90%) protection against severe forms of TB, including TBM and miliary TB, 
if given during the neonatal period. Although neonatal vaccination also provides pr

summary.text: Describes BCG vaccine, which gives up to 90% protection against severe TB forms such as meningitis and miliary TB when given at birth and modest protection against infection. It summarises the WHO position paper recommendations on neonatal vaccination in high-burden settings and special groups. It describes local, regional and disseminated adverse events, including BCG-related immune reconstitution syndrome in people with HIV, and their management.

blocks.content: Close-up photograph illustrating administration of BCG (Figure 3.3): a hand holds a small syringe whose needle is inserted almost flat into the skin of a child's arm, which rests on white cloth.

blocks.title: TB preventive treatment
blocks.content:
3.3.1. Introduction
TB infection (previously called latent TB infection) is defined as a “state of persistent immune response 
to stimulation by M. tuberculosis antigens without evidence of TB disease” (15). The number of people 
worldwide estimated to have M. tuberculosis infection is 1.7 billion. Further, 7.5 million children aged 
under 15 years are estimated to be infected with TB every year (11). By 2014, a cumulative 67 million 
children aged under 15 years were infected with TB, including 2 million with MDR-TB and 100 000 
with XDR-TB strains (12). People with TB infection have no signs

summary.text: Covers TB preventive treatment in children and adolescents, defining TB infection, its global burden and the 5–10% lifetime risk of progression, higher in young children and people with HIV. The headings show it addresses target groups for preventive treatment, ruling out TB disease, testing for infection, the available regimens and child-friendly formulations, and practical implementation. A table explains how to manage missed doses for different regimens such as 3HP and 1HP. It ends by referring other issues, such as babies born to women with TB and ART choice, to other sections and the Module 1 handbook.

blocks.title: TB infection prevention and control
blocks.content:
The End TB Strategy emphasizes the need for prevention across all efforts to end the TB epidemic, 
including infection prevention and control in health care services and other high-transmission settings (7). 
Infection prevention and control practices are critical to reduce the risk of M. tuberculosis transmission, 
by reducing the concentration of infectious droplet nuclei in the air and the exposure of susceptible 
people to such aerosols. Although the recommendations in the WHO guidelines on tuberculosis infection 
prevention and control: 2019 update do not specifically mention children or

summary.text: Explains TB infection prevention and control in health facilities, noting that adolescents can transmit like adults and that poor practices expose children, and that COVID-19 mask use may reduce stigma. It outlines administrative, environmental and respiratory protection measures and closes with key points on prevention.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Diagnostic evaluation is the step in the care cascade after screening. Children and adolescents who 
screen positive during contact investigation or at health facility-based screening, and those who 
present to a health care facility with signs and symptoms of TB and who are identified as having 
presumptive TB must be evaluated further for TB disease.
The diagnosis of TB disease is usually made based on careful clinical assessment, supported by 
relevant tests and investigations. Most young children with TB have paucibacillary disease, meaning 
they harbour relatively few TB bacilli. Conseque

summary.text: Introduces the diagnostic chapter, explaining that children with presumptive TB need careful clinical assessment and that bacteriological confirmation is hard in young children because of few bacilli and difficulty producing sputum.

blocks.title: TB diagnostic approaches for children and adolescents
blocks.content:
with drug-susceptible TB, DR-TB, PTB and EPTB. PTB is the most common type of TB in children and 
adolescents. in children usually involves disease in the intrathoracic lymph nodes, but in adolescents 
it more commonly resembles adult-type disease with cavitary lesions (4, 6). This chapter relates to 
the section of the pathway highlighted in blue in Figure 4.1.

blocks.title: Diagnosing TB in children and adolescents

summary.text: Lists the groups of children and adolescents at highest risk of TB disease, such as close contacts, under-fives and those with HIV or severe malnutrition, from the WHO operational handbook on TB in children and adolescents. It sets out the components of diagnosis, including history, examination, HIV testing, bacteriological testing and chest X-ray, and advises against a trial of TB treatment as a diagnostic method.

blocks.title: Diagnostic approaches: pulmonary TB
blocks.content:
PTB refers to any bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB involving the 
lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree. Tuberculous mediastinal and/or hilar intrathoracic 
lymphadenopathy is also classified as PTB, following an expert consultation convened by WHO in 
September 2021.15 Miliary TB is classified as PTB because there are lesions in the lungs. Tuberculous 
pleural effusion without radiographic abnormalities in the lungs constitutes EPTB. A person with both 
PTB and EPTB should be classified as having PTB (71).
4.3.1. Typical symptoms of pulmonary TB
In most cases,

summary.text: Defines pulmonary TB in children, including intrathoracic lymph node and miliary disease, and describes typical persistent symptoms, cough patterns and the importance of a TB contact history. It covers clinical examination signs suggestive of pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB and considerations during contact investigation. The section goes on to cover diagnostic tests and treatment decision algorithms for children who cannot be confirmed bacteriologically. It ends with an example of scoring under Algorithm B and definitions of the symptoms used in the algorithms, such as cough, fever, weight loss and tachycardia.

blocks.title: Diagnostic approaches: extrapulmonary TB
blocks.content:
EPTB refers to any bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed case of TB involving organs other 
than the lungs (e.g. pleura, peripheral lymph nodes, abdomen, genitourinary tract, skin, joints and 
bones, meninges) (71). The classification of intrathoracic lymphadenopathy in children was updated 
following an expert consultation in September 2021 as PTB. EPTB is common in young children 
and in children and adolescents living with HIV. Since it is more difficult to diagnose, children with 
presumed EPTB, especially those who are very ill, should be urgently evaluated or referred for f

summary.text: Defines extrapulmonary TB in children and notes it is common in young children and those with HIV, calling for urgent evaluation or referral of very ill children. It reproduces WHO recommendations on using Xpert MTB/RIF and Ultra on non-respiratory specimens such as CSF, lymph node aspirates and blood. A table lists typical presentations and investigations for different extrapulmonary sites, such as TB meningitis, miliary and abdominal TB.

blocks.title: Disease severity
blocks.content:
In children and adolescents, severity of TB disease ranges from mild to severe. Children with non-
severe, drug-susceptible TB are now eligible to receive a shortened 4-month treatment regimen. 
For consideration of a 4-month treatment regimen for non-severe, drug-susceptible PTB in children 
and young adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years, non-severe TB is defined based on the clinical 
presentation of disease as assessed through physical examination and CXR. All children who have a 
decision to treat for PTB based on the treatment decision algorithms should be assessed for disease 
severity.

summary.text: Explains how TB disease severity is assessed in children, since those aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe drug-susceptible TB can receive a shorter 4-month regimen. It defines non-severe disease by clinical and chest X-ray findings and stresses that assessing severity should not delay treatment.

blocks.title: Diagnostic approaches: drug-resistant TB
blocks.content:
The clinical presentation of DR-TB in a child or adolescent is similar to that of other forms of TB in a child 
or adolescent. When DR-TB is suspected, it is important to collect respiratory samples (stool, expectorated 
or induced sputum, NPA sample or gastric aspirate) for bacteriological confirmation by Xpert MTB/RIF or 
Xpert Ultra when possible. Truenat MTB or MTB Plus may also be used for sputum specimens. Xpert and 
Truenat assays provide rapid information that indicates rifampicin resistance and therefore DR-TB. Culture-
based phenotypic DST, rapid, low-complexity automated nucleic aci

summary.text: Describes how to diagnose drug-resistant TB in children, emphasizing collection of respiratory or stool samples for rapid molecular tests that detect rifampicin resistance and the role of source-case information. It reproduces WHO recommendations on molecular tests for resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones and other drugs. Key messages stress prioritizing bacteriological testing for all children with presumed TB.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
This chapter summarizes the treatment options available for children and adolescents to treat drug-
susceptible TB and DR-TB and pulmonary and extrapulmonary forms of TB (including TBM), and 
considerations related to post-TB health. It includes operational guidance on various new treatment 
approaches, including a 4-month treatment regimen, and important implementation considerations such 
as availability of child-friendly formulations and access to all key medicines for the treatment of DR-TB.
Treatment outcomes for children completing TB treatment are generally excellent. The vast majority

summary.text: Introduces the treatment chapter, which covers regimens for drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB, TB meningitis and post-TB health, including the new 4-month regimen. It notes that treatment outcomes in children are generally excellent and that most child TB deaths occur in those never treated, with a figure illustrating the cascade from exposure to treatment.

blocks.title: Treatment of drug-susceptible TB in children and adolescents

summary.text: Sets out the principles of managing drug-susceptible TB in children and adolescents, from medicine management and comorbidities to family involvement, adherence support and recording. It describes the recommended regimens, including the 4-month regimen for non-severe TB based on the SHINE trial, the rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen for adolescents aged 12 and over, and a 6-month intensive regimen for TB meningitis. It also covers child-friendly fixed-dose formulations, dose adjustment as children gain weight, adverse events and monitoring. Key messages summarize these points and require all children treated for TB to be registered and reported to the national TB programme.

blocks.title: Treatment of multidrug-resistant and rifampicin-resistant TB in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
resistant TB in children and adolescents
This section describes a practical approach to the treatment of children with rifampicin-resistant 
tuberculosis (RR-TB) and MDR-TB (resistant to both rifampicin and isoniazid). It covers identifying 
children who should be treated for MDR/RR-TB, deciding on the most appropriate treatment regimen, 
monitoring, and other implementation issues related to treatment.
5.3.1. Identifying children who should be treated for 
multidrug-resistant and rifampicin-resistant TB
Based on modelling estimates, between 25 000 and 32 000 children and young adolescents age

summary.text: Describes the practical treatment of children with multidrug- and rifampicin-resistant TB, starting with estimates that tens of thousands of children develop MDR-TB each year yet few are diagnosed. It presents the WHO drug groupings and recommendations favouring the shorter all-oral bedaquiline regimen or individualized longer regimens, now with bedaquiline and delamanid allowed at all ages. It covers monitoring, adverse events and implementation issues. Key messages call for specimen collection, empirical treatment based on the source case, child-friendly formulations, avoiding injectables and social support for families.

blocks.title: Practical guidance for assessment and management of post-TB health in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
management of post-TB health in children and 
adolescents
5.4.1. Post-TB health
Awareness of the consequences of TB disease in children and adolescents that go beyond survival and 
completion of treatment has increased (131, 132). Each child or adolescent on TB treatment should 
be assigned a mutually exclusive treatment outcome at the end of treatment, but follow-up and care 
may need to go beyond the conclusion of TB treatment (71). There is also a need to quantify and 
monitor the burden of morbidity that occurs after TB treatment has been completed (post-TB health). 
Improved data on post-

summary.text: Introduces post-TB health in children and adolescents, noting that consequences of TB can persist after treatment and need to be measured and managed. It describes long-term complications of TB meningitis, such as neurodisability, blindness and hormonal problems, with an end-of-treatment assessment table. It also covers assessment of post-TB lung disease using imaging and spirometry and tools for measuring health-related quality of life in children.

blocks.title: Models of TB care for children and adolescents
blocks.content: and adolescents

summary.text: A section heading fragment on models of TB care for children and adolescents.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
In high TB burden countries, the capacity to manage TB in children and adolescents is often centralized 
at the tertiary or secondary level of health care rather than being decentralized at the PHC level where 
children and adolescents with TB or TB exposure commonly seek care (5, 157). Care at higher levels 
in the health system is often managed in a vertical, non-integrated way. Children and adolescents 
with TB may go undetected because of missed opportunities for contact investigation, TB prevention, 
detection and care, and as a result of weak integration of child and adolescent TB servic

summary.text: Explains that TB care for children in high-burden countries is often centralized and poorly integrated with child health, nutrition and HIV services, leading to missed cases and delays. It cites the 2018 Roadmap's key action on community engagement. It then reproduces WHO recommendations on decentralized, family-centred and integrated care and on community-based, lay-provider and video-supported treatment support.

blocks.title: Decentralized, family-centred, integrated TB services
blocks.content:
services
Decentralization includes the provision of, access to or capacity for child and adolescent TB services 
at a lower level of the health system than the lowest level where it is currently routinely provided. In 
most settings, decentralization applies to the district hospital level (first referral level), PHC level or 
community level. Interventions to facilitate decentralization include capacity-building of various cadres 
of HCWs, access to diagnostic services, availability of TB medicines for children and adolescents, and 
follow-up of children and adolescents with TB or on TPT.
Sinc

summary.text: Explains what decentralizing child and adolescent TB services means and the interventions needed, such as training health workers, access to diagnostics and medicines, and follow-up. It describes a flexible approach for national programmes, health workforce tasks at each level of care in a table, and integration with other child health services. The section includes country examples, such as integrating childhood TB into IMNCI services in Addis Ababa with a sharp rise in contact screening and preventive treatment. It notes that services including gastric aspiration can be decentralized to primary care with supporting packages.

blocks.title: Private-sector involvement in care for children and adolescents with TB
blocks.content:
and adolescents with TB
6.3.1. Background
In many high TB burden countries, the majority of missing people with TB, including children, seek 
treatment from private providers or other care providers not linked to the public sector at least once 
(174). The private sector is also a common point of care for children presenting with common illnesses, 
such as cough, fever and diarrhoea, especially in countries with a large private sector (175). In these 
countries, people with or at risk of TB are unlikely to access good-quality TB services if the NTP does 
not comprehensively engage the private

summary.text: Explains that many children with TB first seek care from private providers and that national programmes must engage the private sector. It sets out key actions from the WHO public–private mix roadmap applied to child TB, such as mapping providers, setting targets, funding and working with paediatric associations. A case study from India describes linking over 1100 children treated by private providers to free public fixed-dose combinations, with the proportion rising from 29% to 65%. It also notes challenges such as treatment delays, pharmacy hours and pill burden.

blocks.title: Differentiated TB service delivery
blocks.content:
6.4.1. Background
The concept of DSD (previously referred to as differentiated care) is increasingly being applied during 
the provision of comprehensive HIV services (78). In the context of HIV, DSD is a people-centred 
approach that simplifies and adapts HIV services to better serve the needs of people living with HIV 
and to optimize the available resources in health systems. DSD is premised on the fact that delivery 
of services is not a one-size-fits-all model but rather recognizes the diversity of people who seek 
the services. It is designed to efficiently deliver people-centred package

summary.text: Introduces differentiated service delivery, a people-centred approach developed for HIV care, and how it can be applied to TB services for children and adolescents. It discusses aligning TB treatment and preventive therapy with multimonth antiretroviral dispensing and family-centred care, while noting risks of fewer screening opportunities. Illustrated examples show models for children receiving TB preventive treatment, such as a child contact of a caregiver with HIV and TB supported by SMS.

blocks.title: TB and health emergencies
blocks.content:
Health emergencies, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, are associated with a disruption in health 
service delivery, either directly due to the focused attention given to the emergency or indirectly due 
to measures implemented to control the emergency.
The COVID-19 pandemic has reversed years of progress in providing essential TB services and 
reducing the disease burden of TB. There has been a large global drop in the number of people 
newly diagnosed with TB and reported. The number fell from 7.1 million in 2019 to 5.8 million (out 
of the approximately 10 million people estimated to have devel

summary.text: Describes how health emergencies such as COVID-19 disrupted TB services, citing the fall in notified TB cases from 7.1 million in 2019 to 5.8 million in 2020. It discusses the direct and indirect effects of emergencies on child and adolescent TB services and outlines measures to maintain care. It concludes that mitigation approaches should take account of the particular needs of children and adolescents with or exposed to TB.

blocks.content:
This chapter covers a range of special situations related to the management of TB in children 
and adolescents:

summary.text: Introduces the chapter on special situations in managing TB in children and adolescents.

blocks.title: Management of TB in children and adolescents living with HIV

summary.text: Lists the special situations covered in the chapter and opens section 7.1 on TB in children and adolescents living with HIV, who face higher risks of TB infection, disease and death. It covers HIV testing recommendations, TB screening with symptom screening and chest radiography, and prevention through preventive treatment for household contacts. Later parts address treatment and co-management with antiretroviral therapy. It ends with guidance on recognising and managing TB immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, including when to continue treatment, use anti-inflammatory drugs or refer.

blocks.title: TB in pregnancy and management of newborns of mothers with TB disease
blocks.content:
of mothers with TB disease
TB contributes to 6–15% of all maternal mortality and leads to adverse pregnancy outcomes (187). 
A national registry study found incidence rate ratios for TB in pregnant and postpartum women of 
1.4 and 1.9, respectively, compared with non-pregnant women (188). TB in pregnancy is associated 
with adverse maternal outcomes and complications during birth, such as pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, 
vaginal bleeding, hospitalization and miscarriage. Perinatal outcomes include a two-fold increased 
risk of premature birth, low birthweight and intrauterine growth retardation, and

summary.text: Describes the contribution of TB to maternal mortality and adverse pregnancy and perinatal outcomes, and covers TB screening for pregnant women living with HIV with a table of screening tool accuracy. It then addresses diagnosis and management of congenital and neonatal TB. It closes with care for well newborns of mothers with TB, including preventive treatment, referral for MDR/RR-TB exposure and infection control.

blocks.title: Palliative care for children and adolescents with TB
blocks.content:
7.3.1. Introduction
In 2014, World Health Assembly Resolution WHA67.19 called upon WHO and Member States to 
improve access to palliative care as a core component of health systems, with an emphasis on PHC 
and community- and home-based care (197). WHO is supporting integration of palliative care into 
all relevant global disease control and health system plans and is promoting improved access to 
palliative care for children, in collaboration with the United Nations Children’s Fund.
	
Î Assess the newborn. If the newborn is not well, refer to a specialist or paediatrician for 
further evaluat

summary.text: Covers palliative care for children and adolescents with TB, starting from the 2014 World Health Assembly resolution calling for better access to palliative care. It describes circumstances in which children with TB may need palliative care and actions to make it available. A table gives examples of managing symptoms such as breathlessness and cough in children with advanced lung disease.

blocks.content: Infographic titled 'What is palliative care?' (Figure 7.1): a stylized tree whose branches point to six statements – it is care for patients with life-threatening illnesses and their families; it can be given in homes, health centres, hospitals and hospices; it improves quality of life; it benefits health systems by reducing unnecessary hospital admissions; it relieves physical, psychosocial and spiritual suffering; it can be done by many types of health professionals and volunteers.

blocks.title: Care for adolescents with or at risk of TB
blocks.content:
Adolescents with TB often present with bacteriologically infectious disease typical in adults (e.g. 
cavities seen on CXR) and therefore pose a high risk for transmission in households and congregate 
settings such as schools. Adolescents face unique challenges due to peer pressure and fear of stigma, 
increasing prevalence of comorbidities such as HIV, and risk behaviours such as use of alcohol, tobacco 
and other substances. People aged 10–19 years need adolescent-friendly services that include relevant 
psychosocial support and minimal disruption of education (5).
Age-disaggregated data on

summary.text: Describes the needs of adolescents with TB, who often have infectious adult-type disease and face stigma, peer pressure, comorbidities and risk behaviours. Sections follow a framework of physical and mental health, connectedness, safety and support, education and skills, agency and resilience, and substance use with late presentation to care. Each area sets out actions for adolescent-friendly services. The block ends by calling for collaboration with other sectors on basic needs such as food security and continued schooling.

blocks.title: TB in children with severe acute pneumonia
blocks.content:
TB is a common cause or comorbidity in children with clinically diagnosed pneumonia. A systematic 
review on TB in acute respiratory infection found that M. tuberculosis was identified in around 5–10% of 
children with pneumonia aged under 5 years in TB endemic countries (223). Limited data from clinical 
and autopsy studies suggest that TB was also associated with mortality in these children. Prevalence 
studies, including the multisite PERCH study (224), confirm these findings.
The review found that clinical features, including persistence of symptoms, had low specificity for 
diagnosis of T

summary.text: Discusses TB as a cause or comorbidity of severe pneumonia in young children, citing a systematic review finding TB in about 5-10% of under-fives with pneumonia in endemic countries. It notes that clinical features have low specificity, and includes boxes on implications for implementation and findings of the TB-Speed Pneumonia study on Xpert Ultra testing.

blocks.title: Management of children with TB and malnutrition
blocks.content:
malnutrition
7.6.1. Introduction
By reducing cell-mediated immunity, undernutrition increases the risk of TB, while the catabolic effect 
of TB disease results in weight loss and wasting, creating a vicious cycle (105, 228). Globally, about 45% 
of deaths in children aged under 5 years are attributable to undernutrition (228). Undernutrition may 
be acute or chronic and categorized as moderate or severe. Data from the 2021 Global Tuberculosis 
Report suggest that 1.9 million TB cases per year (19%) are attributable to undernourishment (1). 
Data on TB prevalence among acutely malnourished chil

summary.text: Explains the two-way link between undernutrition and TB in children, citing estimates that about 19% of TB cases are attributable to undernourishment and varied TB prevalence among acutely malnourished children. It covers diagnosis and treatment of TB in malnourished children and nutritional care for children and adolescents with TB. Key points include evaluating children with severe acute malnutrition who fail to gain weight for TB and using a 6-month regimen for them.

blocks.title: Annex 2. Tuberculin skin testing: administration, reading and interpretation
blocks.content:
administration, reading and 
interpretation
This annex provides information on administering, reading and interpreting tuberculin skin tests (TSTs).
A TST is the intradermal injection of a combination of mycobacterial antigens that elicit a delayed-type 
hypersensitivity immune response, represented by induration, which can be measured in millimetres.
The standard method of identifying people infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the TST using 
the Mantoux method. Multiple puncture tests should not be used as these tests are unreliable (because 
the amount of tuberculin injected intrader

summary.text: An annex explaining how to give, read and interpret a tuberculin skin test by the Mantoux method using 5 tuberculin units. It covers the injection technique, measuring induration and thresholds for a positive result. It also discusses causes of false-positive and false-negative results.

blocks.title: Annex 5. Treatment decision algorithms
blocks.content:
algorithms 
Methodology for developing the treatment decision 
algorithms
Individual-level participant diagnostic evaluations and outcome data in children aged under 10 years 
presenting for evaluation of PTB were solicited from studies carried out in geographically diverse high 
TB burden settings. Missing data were imputed using multiple imputations by chained equations. 
Prediction models were built to classify participants as having TB (confirmed or unconfirmed TB) 
or unlikely TB using features from clinical evaluation and CXR as predictors. The predictors were 
selected based on those co

summary.text: An annex presenting treatment decision algorithms for children under 10 with suspected pulmonary TB, starting with how the scoring models were built from pooled individual patient data and set at 85% sensitivity. It explains the triage steps for danger signs, high-risk children and rapid molecular testing that come before scoring. Two algorithms are shown, one for settings with chest X-ray and one without, assigning points to symptoms and radiographic features with a threshold of more than 10 for starting treatment. Operational guidance follows, including age-specific definitions of signs such as fast breathing and a worked scoring example.
